### What issue are you seeing?

With `approval_policy = "on-request"` and `approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"`, commands the model submits with `"sandbox_permissions":"require_escalated"` are **executed inside the Windows sandbox anyway**. No auto-review decision is logged and no approval prompt is shown. Commands that match an exec-policy `prefix_rule(..., decision="allow")` behave the same way.

Evidence from one thread (`01a13f92-7feb-7163-99d3-cf7225789077`):

- 74 of 79 `exec_command` calls requested `require_escalated` with a justification.
- `logs_2.sqlite` contains 23 `codex_guardian_v2::async_scorer::approval ... reviewing approval decision_source="synchronous_assessment" reason=FreshRequired` entries, all between 12:55 and 13:07 UTC, while the daemon was still 0.160.0. After the daemon moved to 0.162.1 (about 13:19 UTC), 39 more `require_escalated` calls produced **no guardian entries at all**, and the rollout has no approval events.
- The "escalated" commands demonstrably ran sandboxed:

| UTC | Escalated request | Observed result |
|---|---|---|
| 12:47 | Maven/Java run | `user.home = C:\Users\CodexSandboxOffline` |
| 12:56 | screenshot via `Graphics.CopyFromScreen` | `The handle is invalid` (sandbox user has no interactive desktop) |
| 14:11 | `SetCursorPos` probe (MXC enabled via `prefer_mxc`) | `SetCursorPos = False`, `GetLastError = 5`, `TokenIsAppContainer = 1` |

Second thread (`01a141b9-8003-7cd1-a957-4d585234048d`, elevated backend, 0.162.1). User rule `prefix_rule(pattern=["gh", "auth", "status"], decision="allow")` is in `~/.codex/rules/default.rules`, and the model also sent `require_escalated` plus `prefix_rule`:

```
exec_command({cmd:"gh auth status","sandbox_permissions":"require_escalated", "prefix_rule":["gh","auth","status"], ...})
-> Failed to create unified exec process: orchestrator_helper_incomplete: setup helper exited successfully before setup completed
(retry)
github.com
  X Failed to log in to github.com account <user> (default)
  - The token in default is invalid.
gh pr list -> HTTP 401: Requires authentication
```

The logs show these calls going through the sandbox managed network proxy (`codex.network_proxy.policy_decision ... server.address="api.github.com" client.address="127.0.0.1:..."`). The gh token sits in the user's Windows Credential Manager, which the sandbox user cannot read. Outside Codex, the same `gh auth status` succeeds from the same pwsh binary.

`codex execpolicy check --rules ~/.codex/rules/default.rules -- gh auth status` returns `"decision":"allow"`.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Windows 11, Codex CLI 0.162.1 with the app-server daemon, `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"` (also reproduced with `[features] prefer_mxc = true`).
2. `config.toml`: `approval_policy = "on-request"`, `approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"`, a permission profile based on `:workspace` (`default_permissions = "<profile>"` with `extends = ":workspace"`).
3. Log in with `gh auth login` (keyring storage), and optionally add `prefix_rule(pattern=["gh", "auth", "status"], decision="allow")`.
4. Ask Codex to run `gh auth status`, or any command that needs the real user (desktop access, user credential store).
5. The model sends `require_escalated`. The command runs as `CodexSandboxOnline`/`CodexSandboxOffline` (elevated) or in an AppContainer (MXC). There is no guardian review and no prompt.

Thread ids: `01a13f92-7feb-7163-99d3-cf7225789077`, `01a141b9-8003-7cd1-a957-4d585234048d`.

### What is the expected behavior?

A `require_escalated` request should either go to the configured reviewer (auto-review or the user) and run outside the sandbox when approved, or be rejected with a message the model can see. A command matching an `allow` prefix rule should run outside the sandbox, as described in `on_request_rule_request_permission.md` ("exec-policy allow behavior (including any sandbox bypass) takes precedence"). It should not silently run sandboxed.

### Additional information

- The same setup worked earlier with 0.160.0: guardian reviews were logged. The behavior started after the CLI/daemon update to 0.162.1. The pre-update 12:47 call also ran sandboxed, so 0.160.0 may not have been fully consistent either.
- A separate issue (Windows elevated sandbox re-provisioning loop with repeated UAC prompts) will be filed separately.
- Temporary workaround: `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` / `default_permissions = ":danger-full-access"`.

**Related finding (same machine, thread `01a13ffc-70a0-7c10-86d1-7f921440f18a`):** after resuming an existing thread and choosing **Full Access** via `/permissions`, `thread_settings_applied` shows `active_permission_profile: ":danger-full-access"` and `approval_policy: never`, but `permission_profile.file_system` stays `restricted`: `root: write` plus the 12 deny-read entries (`**\.env*`, `secrets`) carried over from the thread's original profile. The elevated sandbox is therefore still used and fails on a non-admin account:

```
setup refresh: processed 1 write roots (read roots delegated); errors=["write ACE failed on C:\: open ACL target for update"]
Failed to create unified exec process: helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors
failed to load AGENTS.md instructions for environment `local`: fs sandbox helper failed with status exit code: 1: windows sandbox failed: helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors
```

Expected: selecting Full Access drops the old deny entries (unrestricted file system), or at least does not try to ACL the drive root. New threads with `default_permissions = ":danger-full-access"` work.

items.title: Windows: codex exec spawns 16–22 redundant read-only git processes per turn (×3 processes each with Git for Windows)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: exec
labels.description: Issues related to the `codex exec` subcommand

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.162.1 (npm, win32-x64)

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT subscription (not plan-dependent)

### Which model were you using?

gpt-6-luna (default; behaviour is model-independent — no tool calls involved)

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64 (Windows 11), Git for Windows on PATH as `C:\Program Files\Git\cmd\git.exe`

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Non-interactive PowerShell 7 host (scripted `codex exec`)

### Codex doctor report

not included

### What issue are you seeing?

A single `codex exec` turn that makes **no tool calls** spawns **16–22 read-only `git` processes**, mostly the same probes repeated. Traced with `GIT_TRACE2_EVENT` (set only for the `codex` process), in an ordinary repo with commits and an `origin` remote:

| git command (all prefixed `-c safe.bareRepository=explicit -c core.hooksPath=NUL -c core.fsmonitor=false`) | count per turn |
| --- | --- |
| `rev-parse HEAD` | 5 |
| `rev-parse --git-dir` | 3 |
| `rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` | 3 |
| `remote get-url origin` | 3 |
| `remote -v` | 2 |
| `config --null --get core.fsmonitor` | 1 |
| `status --porcelain` | 1 |

HEAD, branch and origin URL are queried 3–5 times each per turn, in waves at session start and turn start (and sometimes at turn end). In an empty repo (`git init`, no commits) it was 22 calls, most `rev-parse` failing with exit 128. A separate process monitor saw up to 27 git invocations in one turn.

On Windows each call goes through the Git for Windows launcher (`cmd\git.exe` → `mingw64\bin\git.exe`) and gets its own `conhost.exe`, so one turn creates **~50–80 short-lived processes** (bursts of ~27 process starts within one second). No windows become visible, but it shows up as a process storm in monitoring tools and costs ~2 s of git time per turn.

Disabling `worktrees`, `workspace_dependencies`, `memories` and `goals` via `-c features.<name>=false` changed the count only marginally (18 → 16). There is no documented setting to turn these probes off.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

```powershell
$env:GIT_TRACE2_EVENT = "$PWD\trace2.jsonl"
codex exec --sandbox read-only --cd <any git repo> "Reply only OK. Do not call tools."
# count git invocations and their argv
Get-Content trace2.jsonl | ConvertFrom-Json | Where-Object event -eq 'start' |
  Group-Object { ($_.argv | Select-Object -Skip 1) -join ' ' } | Sort-Object Count -Descending |
  Format-Table Count, Name -AutoSize
```

### What is the expected behavior?

Git context (HEAD, branch, origin, dirty state) is collected once per turn, or cached per session with invalidation, so a no-tool turn costs a handful of git calls rather than ~20. Optionally, a config switch to disable git context collection.

### Additional information

Possibly related, but not the same: #30635 (app-server loops on `rev-parse --show-toplevel` with an invalid `.git`), #33165 (VS Code extension repeatedly spawning `rev-parse --show-toplevel` in multi-repo workspaces). `undo`/ghost snapshots are already removed in 0.162.1 (`codex features list`), so they are not the source.

items.title: fix(docs): app-server guide documents removed isPinned API

labels.name: documentation
labels.description: Improvements or additions to documentation

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## Summary

The published app-server guide documents an `isPinned` filter, persisted pin updates, and `isPinned` response fields that the current CLI app-server does not implement. Following the guide returns unfiltered thread lists or fails the pin-only update. This is stale documentation after the pinning API was intentionally replaced, rather than a request to add a new pinning feature.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Use the released CLI identified under Runtime or environment. No login or model turn is needed. The script below creates two synthetic rollout fixtures in a temporary home, following the repository's `create_fake_rollout` test-helper format, and uses the documented stdio JSON-RPC transport.
2. Save the script as `repro.py`, set `CODEX_BIN` to the absolute path of that release's `codex` executable, and run `python3 repro.py </dev/null`. It isolates both `HOME` and `CODEX_HOME`, stops the server, and removes its fixtures.

```python
import json
import os
import pathlib
import queue
import shutil
import subprocess
import tempfile
import threading
import uuid

binary = os.environ.get("CODEX_BIN") or shutil.which("codex")
assert binary, "Set CODEX_BIN to the released codex executable"
binary = str(pathlib.Path(binary).resolve())
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="agent-work.", dir="/tmp") as tmp:
    home = pathlib.Path(tmp)
    stamp = subprocess.check_output(
        ["date", "-u", "+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"], text=True
    ).strip()
    folder = home / "sessions" / stamp[:4] / stamp[5:7] / stamp[8:10]
    folder.mkdir(parents=True)
    ids = []
    for n in range(2):
        tid = str(uuid.uuid4())
        ids.append(tid)
        text = f"Synthetic fixture {n + 1}"
        rows = [
            {"timestamp": stamp, "type": "session_meta", "payload": {
                "id": tid, "session_id": tid, "timestamp": stamp, "cwd": "/",
                "originator": "codex", "cli_version": "0.0.0", "source": "cli",
                "model_provider": "openai"}},
            {"timestamp": stamp, "type": "response_item", "payload": {
                "type": "message", "role": "user", "content": [
                    {"type": "input_text", "text": text}]}},
            {"timestamp": stamp, "type": "event_msg", "payload": {
                "type": "user_message", "message": text, "kind": "plain"}},
        ]
        filename = stamp[:19].replace(":", "-")
        (folder / f"rollout-{filename}-{tid}.jsonl").write_text(
            "".join(json.dumps(row) + "\n" for row in rows)
        )
    env = {"PATH": os.environ["PATH"], "HOME": tmp, "CODEX_HOME": tmp}
    with open(os.devnull, "w") as errors:
        proc = subprocess.Popen(
            [binary, "app-server", "--listen", "stdio://"], cwd=tmp, env=env,
            stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=errors,
            text=True, bufsize=1,
        )
        responses = queue.Queue()
        def read():
            for line in proc.stdout:
                responses.put(json.loads(line))
        threading.Thread(target=read, daemon=True).start()
        def send(message):
            proc.stdin.write(json.dumps(message) + "\n")
            proc.stdin.flush()
        def rpc(i, method, params):
            send({"id": i, "method": method, "params": params})
            while True:
                reply = responses.get(timeout=30)
                if reply.get("id") == i:
                    return reply
        def listing(i, extra):
            result = rpc(i, "thread/list", {"limit": 100, **extra})["result"]
            rows = result["data"]
            return {"count": len(rows), "nextCursor": result["nextCursor"],
                    "has_isPinned": any("isPinned" in row for row in rows)}
        try:
            rpc(0, "initialize", {"clientInfo": {
                "name": "pin_docs_repro", "version": "0.0.1"}})
            send({"method": "initialized", "params": {}})
            print("baseline", listing(1, {}))
            print("isPinned=true", listing(2, {"isPinned": True}))
            print("isPinned=false", listing(3, {"isPinned": False}))
            print("pin-only update", rpc(4, "thread/metadata/update", {
                "threadId": ids[0], "isPinned": True}))
            result = rpc(5, "thread/metadata/update", {
                "threadId": ids[0], "isPinned": True,
                "gitInfo": {"branch": "synthetic-branch"}})["result"]["thread"]
            print("pin+gitInfo update", {
                "branch": result["gitInfo"]["branch"],
                "has_isPinned": "isPinned" in result})
            print("after update", listing(6, {"isPinned": True}))
            print("exclusion control", listing(7, {"excludedThreadIds": [ids[0]]}))
        finally:
            proc.stdin.close()
            try:
                proc.wait(timeout=10)
            except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
                proc.terminate()
                proc.wait(timeout=10)
```

## Expected behavior

The guide's “List threads” section describes filtering by persisted pin state, its response examples include `isPinned`, and “Update stored thread metadata” describes changing that state through `thread/metadata/update`. Readers need documentation that matches the supported local CLI protocol, or an explicit surface/version restriction if these examples belong to another server. The same page's getting-started instructions launch `codex app-server`, so these examples currently appear applicable to the tested surface.

## Actual behavior

The executed script prints the following. Both mutually exclusive pin filters return all fixtures. The pin-only update is rejected, and the update combined with valid Git metadata changes only the Git metadata. No returned thread contains `isPinned`. The exclusion control verifies that the same fixture set can be filtered using a supported parameter.

```text
baseline {'count': 2, 'nextCursor': None, 'has_isPinned': False}
isPinned=true {'count': 2, 'nextCursor': None, 'has_isPinned': False}
isPinned=false {'count': 2, 'nextCursor': None, 'has_isPinned': False}
pin-only update {'error': {'code': -32600, 'message': 'thread metadata update must include at least one field'}, 'id': 4}
pin+gitInfo update {'branch': 'synthetic-branch', 'has_isPinned': False}
after update {'count': 2, 'nextCursor': None, 'has_isPinned': False}
exclusion control {'count': 1, 'nextCursor': None, 'has_isPinned': False}
```

## Evidence

- Expected source: The official [Codex App Server guide](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server.md), method overviews, “List threads,” and “Update stored thread metadata.” The fetched Markdown has SHA-256 `f879715bb0d440db60b71e7a5bfe1258d045520feabe3fc6b11847100c8d064b`; the relevant occurrences are lines 300, 308, 479, 483, 728, 758–759, and 770–783.
- Failure source: The executed isolated stdio reproduction and output above; released and current-default-branch protocol definitions omit `isPinned` and `is_pinned`.
- Evidence provenance: observed
- Local verification: reproduced
- Reproduction completeness: complete

The released [`ThreadMetadataUpdateParams` and `ThreadListParams`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/83086188ae0614bd882818ff1aa23f3194962012/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/thread.rs) omit the pin fields. Searching the entire `codex-rs/app-server-protocol` subtree for both spellings also returns no matches on the checked default branch. This is source inspection of the default branch, not an executed default-branch build.

## Runtime or environment

- Runtime: Codex CLI `0.163.0`, downloaded from the official `rust-v0.163.0` release's `codex-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz`; macOS `27.0.1`, arm64; `codex app-server --listen stdio://`; isolated homes and two synthetic local session fixtures; no authentication or model turns.
- Release source revision: `83086188ae0614bd882818ff1aa23f3194962012` (the release-source permalink above).
- Checked default branch: `main` at `16e578dd1ddaf4f5db9cd1f3dbfea0958fd74339`; [current protocol definitions](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/16e578dd1ddaf4f5db9cd1f3dbfea0958fd74339/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/thread.rs).

## Additional context

Documentation issue type: Documentation is incorrect; Example code is not working. The affected location is the official guide linked under Evidence. Its exact current website source was not found in this public repository; the repository's app-server README is a different document and contains no `isPinned` references.

Historical [PR #34840](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/34840) added persisted pinning. [PR #35722](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/35722) intentionally replaced `isPinned` metadata/filtering with sections and corrected the repository README at the same time; that replacement is an ancestor of the tested release. These historical changes explain why the current guide is stale. Neither tracks the present published-documentation mismatch. Tracker searches across open/closed issues and PRs found related desktop pinning requests but no report specifically addressing this guide's removed API; search-index omissions limit completeness.

## Restoration check

Check every pinning claim in the published guide against the protocol shipped for the documented local server. A reader following the corrected list/update instructions should obtain the documented filtering, persistence, and response fields on that server. If an obsolete example remains for a distinct surface or historical version, its applicability must be explicit. Re-run the same fixture scenario with the documented supported API; retain an unfiltered listing and a supported-filter control so an empty history cannot mask the mismatch. This report does not require reintroducing `isPinned`.

## Triage assessment

- Impact level: P2
- Assessment status: supported
- Impact basis: Integration authors following the documented API receive unfiltered history or a rejected pin update, and cannot read the promised response field. The observed failure is bounded to clients using these obsolete documented fields; the local server and ordinary listing remain usable.
- Workaround status: unverified
- Workaround basis: Avoiding `isPinned` prevents reliance on the obsolete examples, and supported exclusions were tested, but exclusions do not supply persisted pinning. Historical source describes sections as the replacement; an equivalent complete pinning workflow was not exercised in this report.

items.title: fix(keymap): leader settings written by /keymap break older shared-config readers

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: TUI
labels.description: Issues related to the terminal user interface: text input, menus and dialogs, and terminal display

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: config
labels.description: Issues involving config.toml, config keys, config merging, or config updates

items.body:
## Summary

`/keymap` exposes leader configuration and symbolic `leader <key>` bindings that its persistence path writes into the root `tui.keymap` configuration. Older readers sharing that configuration reject either representation even without `--strict-config`. This includes the tested CLI bundled with the ChatGPT desktop app: its app-server cannot start a new thread until the incompatible setting is removed or rewritten.

## Steps to reproduce

The following config-load reproduction was executed with each binary listed under Runtime or environment. It uses an isolated, unauthenticated `CODEX_HOME`, a non-Git working directory, stdin from `/dev/null`, and no model turn. Set `CODEX_BIN` to each binary in turn.

```sh
config_home=$(mktemp -d)
work_dir=$(mktemp -d)
printf '[tui.keymap.global]\nleader = "ctrl-x"\n' > "$config_home/config.toml"
(cd "$work_dir" && CODEX_HOME="$config_home" "$CODEX_BIN" debug prompt-input hi </dev/null)
printf 'exit=%s\n' "$?"

# Repeat the same command after replacing config.toml with each fixture:
printf '[tui.keymap.global]\ncopy = ["ctrl-o", "leader c"]\n' > "$config_home/config.toml"
# Compatible control:
printf '[tui.keymap.global]\ncopy = ["ctrl-o", "ctrl-x c"]\n' > "$config_home/config.toml"
```

For the desktop-bundled binary, the server failure was also reproduced over stdio. Start `CODEX_HOME="$config_home" "$CODEX_BIN" app-server` in the isolated working directory, then send these JSON lines in order, waiting for each response before the next request. No `turn/start` request is sent.

```json
{"id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"clientInfo":{"name":"config-probe","version":"1"}}}
{"method":"initialized"}
{"id":2,"method":"config/read","params":{}}
{"id":3,"method":"thread/start","params":{"cwd":"<isolated-work-dir>","ephemeral":true}}
```

Replace `<isolated-work-dir>` with the actual disposable working directory. Repeat with each leader fixture, then with the literal-chord fixture and an empty config.

The UI write path was traced in source, not driven interactively: `/keymap` → Global/leader → change the prefix, or select an action → `Use leader...` → capture a suffix. The direct fixtures above exercise the resulting representations independently of interactive input.

## Expected behavior

A supported `/keymap` edit should preserve usability for the older reader sharing the configuration, or keep an incompatible edit from silently breaking that reader. The keymap action catalog already deliberately excludes another new action from shared-config writes until older strict readers accept it. This report concerns that narrow compatibility intent; it does not assume a general guarantee that arbitrary future configuration works with every past release.

## Actual behavior

| Config fixture | Latest CLI | Previous stable CLI | Desktop-bundled CLI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `leader = "ctrl-x"` | exit 0 | exit 1: unknown field `leader` | same rejection |
| `copy = ["ctrl-o", "leader c"]` | exit 0 | exit 1: unknown key `leader` | same rejection |
| `copy = ["ctrl-o", "ctrl-x c"]` | exit 0 | exit 0 | exit 0 |
| Empty config | exit 0 | exit 0 | exit 0 |

The meaningful errors are:

```text
<isolated-home>/config.toml:2:10: unknown field `leader`, expected one of `open_agents`, `open_transcript`, `find_transcript`, `focus_activity`, `open_external_editor`, `copy`, `clear_terminal`, `submit`, `queue`, `toggle_shortcuts`, `toggle_vim_mode`, `toggle_fast_mode`, `toggle_raw_output`, `toggle_side_conversation`

<isolated-home>/config.toml:2:19: unknown key `leader` in keybinding `leader`. Use a printable character (for example `a`), function keys (`f1`-`f24`), or one of: enter, tab, backspace, esc, delete, arrows, home/end, page-up/page-down, space, minus.
```

For both leader fixtures, the desktop-bundled app-server logs `Invalid configuration; using defaults`, successfully responds to `initialize`, returns error `-32603` from `config/read`, and returns error `-32600` with `failed to load configuration` from `thread/start`. Both requests succeed with the literal-chord and empty-config controls. This verifies the bundled server failure without touching a running desktop app; the GUI itself was not exercised.

## Runtime or environment

- Latest published stable CLI: `codex-cli 0.163.0`, downloaded from the official GitHub release asset `codex-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` under tag `rust-v0.163.0`; release source commit `83086188ae0614bd882818ff1aa23f3194962012`.
- Previous stable CLI: `codex-cli 0.162.1`, downloaded from the same official asset name under tag `rust-v0.162.1`.
- Desktop-bundled CLI: `codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.17.2`, read-only invocation of the CLI shipped in ChatGPT desktop app version `26.1007.71326`, build `20398`.
- Platform: `Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm`; no terminal emulator or multiplexer was used for these noninteractive probes.
- Subscription and model: not applicable; no authentication or model request was used.
- Current default branch inspected in a fresh clone: `main` at `16e578dd1ddaf4f5db9cd1f3dbfea0958fd74339`. This checkout was inspected statically, not compiled or run. Windows/Linux and newer desktop bundles were not tested.
- Codex doctor report: run against an empty disposable home; it reports missing authentication and other environment checks, which do not establish this writer/reader incompatibility. The config-load and app-server results above are the targeted diagnostic evidence.

## Evidence

- Expected source: the release's [keymap catalog compatibility guard and exposed leader action](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/tui/src/keymap_setup/actions.rs#L89-L100), which explicitly withholds the warnings action from shared-config writes for older readers.
- Failure source: locally executed config-load and desktop-bundled app-server probes, with exact fixtures, error messages, and controls above; the latest writer's reachability is supported separately by source inspection below.
- Evidence provenance: observed
- Local verification: reproduced
- Reproduction completeness: complete

The release's [`Use leader...` menu](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/tui/src/keymap_setup.rs#L251-L264) selects leader capture; [`capture.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/tui/src/keymap_setup/capture.rs#L158-L174) turns that capture into `leader {key}` and emits `KeymapCaptured`. [`apply_keymap_capture`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/tui/src/app/event_dispatch.rs#L3508-L3572) validates with its current runtime keymap and passes the bindings to `ConfigEditsBuilder` for the user config path. [`keymap_bindings_edit`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0/codex-rs/core/src/config/edit.rs#L143-L162) writes the exact bindings under `tui.keymap.<context>.<action>`. Editing an already active value can be a no-op; changing the leader prefix or assigning a new symbolic suffix takes the write path.

Current `main` retains the compatibility comment and leader catalog entry in `keymap_setup/actions.rs` at lines 117–127, and retains symbolic capture in `keymap_setup/capture.rs` at line 162. Its [`apply_keymap_capture`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/16e578dd1ddaf4f5db9cd1f3dbfea0958fd74339/codex-rs/tui/src/app/event_dispatch.rs#L3611-L3697) additionally asks an attached local daemon to validate the write, while retaining a direct-write path for other targets. That check protects an attached older daemon; it does not check a separate older app-server that later reads the same file. No current-main fix for this shared-reader case was found.

## Restoration check

Starting from a configuration usable by both readers, make a leader-prefix or symbolic-suffix edit through the newer `/keymap` path. Verify that the older reader still loads the shared config and that its app-server's `config/read` and `thread/start` succeed, or that an unsupported edit is rejected without changing the usable config. Preserve the literal-chord control and the newer reader's functioning bindings so a pass cannot come from merely discarding all keymap configuration.

## Triage assessment

- Impact level: P2
- Assessment status: supported
- Impact basis: A bounded cross-version shared-config edit prevents the tested older CLI from loading configuration and its app-server from starting threads. The failure persists for each load while either incompatible representation remains. The GUI and other platforms were not tested.
- Workaround status: available
- Workaround basis: With the explicit leader field absent, the literal chord `ctrl-x c` loads in all three tested binaries, and both configuration reads and thread creation succeed in the tested bundled app-server. This preserves a fixed chord; symbolic rebinding remains unavailable to the older reader.

items.title: Support remote credential masking with Zsh shell snapshots
items.body:
Support remote credential masking with Zsh shell snapshots

## Why

Remote credential masking previously supported only Bash commands without login startup or shell snapshots, leaving Zsh commands with unmasked credentials.

## What changed

- Enable masking for Zsh login commands using shell snapshots on Linux and macOS.
- Capture trusted startup profiles per launch, bind the credential broker to the resulting environment, and replace credentials and supported aliases with placeholders before snapshot replay.
- Preserve explicit environment overrides, credential unsets, and launcher-managed proxy settings during replay.
- Warn and fall back to unmasked startup when a snapshot cannot safely replay credentials; stop execution if protected snapshot restoration fails.

## Testing

Extend remote execution tests for inherited and profile-defined credentials, overrides, destination changes, and unsupported-profile fallback. Add a Zsh scenario snapshot showing a credential placeholder in command output.

items.title: Provide durable reconciliation for orphaned child turns after process loss

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: subagent
labels.description: Issues involving subagents or multi-agent features

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
# Durable reconciliation for an orphaned V2 child turn

Tracking use case: erickb336/sage#246. Please identify an existing supported recovery contract or consider the operation described below.

Sage needs native evidence that an interrupted child can no longer execute its old turn. A display status alone cannot authorize capacity release or reassignment.

## Observed behavior

The reproduction used the native Codex CLI 0.160.0, an isolated profile, and fixed simulated Responses output. It made no real model calls.

- A clean input shutdown persisted a child interruption record.
- Abrupt loss of the tracked native process left the child transcript without a terminal record through the observed restart phases.
- Resuming the root did not restore the child in the live registry or issue a child model request.
- Loading the saved child through its recorded parent produced a pending child, not a resumed turn. The API displayed the old turn as interrupted; the inspected transcript did not gain a terminal record.

These observations cover that reproduction. They do not establish that every supported recovery path is unavailable.

The reproducible harness is in [Sage PR #247](https://github.com/erickb336/sage/pull/247), at commit `02d306608da424ef6611965fb09426fa70e8a419`. Its [instructions and evidence limits](https://github.com/erickb336/sage/blob/02d306608da424ef6611965fb09426fa70e8a419/docs/verification/codex-active-child-restart.md) distinguish clean EOF, direct native loss, and saved-child loading. Raw captures remain local and contain no real model calls.

## Source audit and version limits

The source audit covers [0.162.1](https://github.com/openai/codex/releases/tag/rust-v0.162.1), commit `092d3acd6bec3e3a14bdc7e7a2810ab628ab759d`. Native reproduction covers 0.160.0 only. At submission, 0.163.0 is the latest published release; it has not been source-audited or native-tested in this investigation.

- [V2 parent interruption](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.1/codex-rs/core/src/agent/control/interrupt.rs#L1) explicitly does not reload an absent child. An unloaded or already-dead runtime can return success. This file is unchanged from 0.160.0.
- [Saved-child loading](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.1/codex-rs/core/src/thread_manager.rs#L1236) requires the recorded immediate parent to be loaded. It delegates to that parent's agent control.
- [Turn interruption](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.1/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/turn_processor.rs#L1610) requires a matching active turn for a normal turn request. The empty-turn startup path does not wait for a turn-aborted event.
- [Response normalization](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.1/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/thread_processor.rs#L5823) changes returned turn statuses when the thread is not active. That function does not persist a terminal record.
- [Persistence resume](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.1/codex-rs/thread-store/src/local/live_writer.rs#L40) selects history under writer ownership, then opens the existing recorder. The [recorder resume branch](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.1/codex-rs/rollout/src/recorder.rs#L995) starts with no pending items.
- The [active task abort path](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.1/codex-rs/core/src/tasks/mod.rs#L1015) emits an exact turn-aborted event and flushes it. It requires the live task being aborted.

The inspected paths do not establish a durable settlement contract for an old turn with no live task. The newer history-revision check improves replay freshness; it is not a crash receipt.

## Requested contract

Please identify an existing supported operation, or consider a parent-owned reconciliation operation, with these guarantees:

1. Bind the persisted result to the recorded root, immediate parent, child, and exact old turn. Sage can then join those native identifiers to its immutable assignment.
2. Establish exclusive authority before settling the old execution. Refuse a competing writer, changed history, foreign parent, or uncertain live owner.
3. Persist a distinct interruption or crash-reconciliation outcome before returning success. Do not fabricate a report or successful completion.
4. Make retries idempotent. Preserve the old history, and reject a conflicting request or later turn.
5. Require no child model turn, prepared follow-up, prompt injection, or direct edit of the saved transcript.
6. Document incomplete storage-write behavior and the boundary of the guarantee across local processes, remote hosts, and copied profiles.

## Current consumer behavior

Recommendation: retain the reservation and request supported native reconciliation evidence.

An alternative would be an explicit abandonment operation with its own outcome and a guarantee against overlapping execution. Sage has not implemented that policy. A missing process, elapsed time, API display status, or successful no-op interrupt is not enough.

This request is separate from fail-closed hook activation and trusted tool execution-context capture.

items.title: Expose trusted resolved execution context to policy hooks

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: hooks
labels.description: Issues related to event hooks

items.body:
# Trusted resolved execution context for policy hooks

Tracking use case: erickb336/sage#243. This request concerns a supported runtime contract for policy extensions. It is separate from required-hook failure handling in #41979.

Related reports: #32360 and #50271 cover effective working directory; #40996 covers permission context. This request brings those needs together with executor identity, filesystem namespace, shell resolution, and per-call freshness. If an existing supported interface covers them, please point us to it.

## Problem

A policy hook needs the settings that the executor will actually use. Original model arguments do not establish those settings. A hook cannot safely infer execution paths from its own environment when a command selects a different working directory, shell, or remote executor.

In rust-v0.162.1, the exec_command PreToolUse payload contains the command string. The hook cwd uses the local environment cwd, with the turn cwd as fallback. These fields do not attest the pending command's resolved execution context.

Sources checked:
- https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.1/codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/unified_exec/exec_command.rs#L514
- https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.1/codex-rs/core/src/tools/registry.rs#L609
- https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.1/codex-rs/core/src/hook_runtime.rs#L248

## Requested capability

Provide a supported, versioned policy interface for the resolved operation before execution. An extension to an existing hook or a separate runtime callback could satisfy this request. The interface must bind evidence to the authenticated session, actor, turn, and exact tool call.

Required evidence or equivalent trusted checks:

- Selected executor and filesystem namespace, including whether execution is local or remote.
- Effective working directory after resolving omitted, empty, relative, and explicit inputs.
- Effective shell executable, shell type, and invocation/login behavior.
- The lookup settings needed for executable and path policy, including PATH, HOME, and CDPATH, without exposing credentials or a full environment dump.
- Effective sandbox and permission policy, including permitted additions and inherited settings.
- A supported way to evaluate relevant filesystem, symlink, executable identity, and checkout evidence in that same namespace.

Specify when evidence is captured, how rewrites affect it, and what invalidates an earlier decision. A changed executor, directory, permission setting, or operation must require a fresh decision. Evidence for one call must not authorize another. Successful extension policy must preserve native sandbox and approval checks.

The interface must state its limits. Shell startup scripts and arbitrary programs can change behavior after this point. Context metadata is not proof that a command is harmless and does not replace a filesystem sandbox.

## Validation examples

1. Compare omitted and explicit workdir inputs with the command's actual directory in an isolated fixture.
2. Compare requested shell strings with the runtime-selected executable and invocation.
3. Exercise inherited and explicit permission settings without bypassing native approvals.
4. Verify local and remote namespaces; local filesystem inspection must not stand in for remote evidence.
5. Refuse mismatched session, actor, turn, or call identities, stale snapshots, and changed operations.
6. Verify denial prevents the operation. Separately cover hook timeout, exception, and transport failure through the fail-closed contract.

## Current Sage boundary

Sage can recover original requested arguments from protected native transcripts. Its verified fixture path does not establish a complete installed evaluator. Automatic activation remains disabled. Native probes with simulated model responses establish only the behavior they directly observe.

## Evidence limits

The source audit covers rust-v0.162.1. At submission, rust-v0.163.0 is the latest published release; it has not been source-audited or native-tested in this investigation. The cited 0.162.1 source was read directly. This request does not claim a new native comparison run or that every possible runtime interface was exhaustively excluded.

Sage needs a supported producer or a separately designed execution boundary. Model-supplied fields cannot supply runtime authority.

items.title: Managed Cloud: local AF_UNIX socketpair send fails with EPERM and hangs asyncio/AnyIO

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: codex-web
labels.description: Issues related to Codex Web

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

items.body:
## Summary

In a managed Codex Cloud task started from a published environment snapshot, a send on a process-local AF_UNIX socket pair raises `PermissionError: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted`. Python asyncio/AnyIO cross-thread completion then hangs.

The worker finishes its function, but the completion callback remains queued while the main event loop waits in the selector. Minimal asyncio and AnyIO probes reproduce the blocked wakeup without application code.

## Minimal operation to reproduce

Equivalent minimal diagnostic:

```python
import socket

a, b = socket.socketpair(socket.AF_UNIX, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
try:
    print(a.send(b"\0"))
finally:
    a.close()
    b.close()
```

Observed in the affected task: the send raises EPERM.
Expected: sending one byte on this already-connected, process-local socket pair succeeds.

The diagnostic retained guards rejecting TCP connection entry points; those guards did not modify socket.send. The origin of the EPERM refusal has not been established.

## Scope and limitations

- This was observed during the agent phase of a new managed Cloud task using a published snapshot.
- The same Python test suite completed in the preparation task before publication but did not complete after restoration.
- A second new task has not been tested; this report does not establish that all Cloud tasks are affected.
- The standalone CLI/runtime version was not collected.
- No security controls or dependencies were changed to bypass the issue.

## Related reports

#24933 and #33793 describe very similar asyncio wakeup and Unix-socket-send symptoms in the Linux CLI sandbox. #53187 describes other socket-related EPERM failures in managed Cloud.

These are symptom matches, not proof of a shared implementation cause.

Please investigate whether managed Cloud execution is affected by the same restriction, and provide a supported resolution that preserves isolation.

This public report intentionally excludes account details, task/feedback identifiers, private environment names, filesystem paths, source code, and raw logs.

items.title: Custom provider: failed previous-model compaction pins the thread to an unavailable model; switching models, resume and fork all keep failing

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: custom-model
labels.description: Issues related to custom model providers (including local models)

labels.name: context
labels.description: Issues related to context management (including compaction)

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

0.155.1 (code paths below are unchanged on rust-v0.163.0)

### What subscription do you have?

None: custom OpenAI-compatible Responses provider (`model_providers` entry with its own base_url and bearer auth)

### Which model were you using?

gpt-6-astra -> gpt-6.1-sol (also gpt-6-sol, gpt-5.5)

### What platform is your computer?

Linux x86_64

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

`codex app-server` with the TUI attached through `codex resume --remote`, inside tmux

### Codex doctor report

```json
not available (diagnosed from Codex's stderr logs)
```

### What issue are you seeing?

After one failed turn on a model that the provider rejects, the thread is stuck permanently. Every later turn first runs pre-turn compaction on that model, gets the same rejection, and ends with `Failed to run pre-sampling compact`. This happens whichever model the user selects. Resuming or forking the thread doesn't help.

In our case model A (`gpt-6-astra`) was rejected with a non-retryable `403 PERMISSION_DENIED` (the provider's spending limit for that model was reached), and model B (`gpt-6.1-sol`) worked.

- Turn on A: sampling fails with the 403. This is expected.
- User switches back to B with `/model` (also tried `gpt-6-sol` and `gpt-5.5`). On every turn, every request goes to A and returns 403, then:

```text
ERROR codex_core::session::turn: Failed to run pre-sampling compact
```

  No request on B is ever made. The thread stays stuck for every turn after that (7 turns over about 50 minutes in our case).
- Fork of the thread (rollout copied, resumed on B):

```text
WARN codex_core::session: resuming session with different model: previous=gpt-6-astra, current=gpt-6.1-sol
```

  The first turn then makes 8 compaction requests to A (all 403) and fails the same way. A separate request to B in the same process returned 200, so B itself was reachable.

A fresh thread built from a plain transcript (no prior `turn_context` naming A) works on B.

### Root cause (source at `rust-v0.163.0`)

1. `maybe_run_previous_model_inline_compact` (`codex-rs/core/src/session/turn.rs`) compacts with `previous_turn_settings.model` whenever the `comp_hash` differs (`CompHashChanged`) or the new model has a smaller context window (`ModelDownshift`).
2. The only current-model retry is `should_retry_with_current_model` (`codex-rs/core/src/compact_model_fallback.rs`). It is used only on the remote-compaction-v2 path. It also requires `current.provider.info().is_openai()` and either Codex-backend or API-key auth. A custom provider without remote compaction goes through `run_inline_auto_compact_task` (`compact.rs`), which never retries. So for these providers, a failed compaction on the previous model is always fatal to the turn.
3. `run_turn` updates `previous_turn_settings` only after `run_pre_sampling_compact` succeeds. When compaction fails, the turn returns `Ok(None)` and the previous model stays A. But a turn that passes compaction records its model as previous before sampling. So a single turn on A whose sampling fails is enough to set the trap.
4. On resume or fork, `rollout_reconstruction.rs` restores `previous_turn_settings` from the newest `turn_context`. A copied rollout therefore inherits A.
5. Manual `/compact` runs on the current model but doesn't update `previous_turn_settings`, so it doesn't clear the state.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Use a custom (non-OpenAI) provider in which model A will reject requests with a permanent error, such as a 403 for quota or permission, while model B works. The models' catalog `comp_hash` values must differ, or A must have a larger context window than B with the history over B's auto-compact limit.
2. In a thread on B, switch to A with `/model` and send a message. Sampling fails, which is expected. `previous_turn_settings` now names A.
3. Switch back to B and send a message. Pre-turn compaction runs on A, fails, logs `Failed to run pre-sampling compact`, and the turn ends.
4. Send more messages, or switch to any other model. Step 3 repeats on every turn.
5. Restart and resume the thread, or fork it. Codex warns `resuming session with different model: previous=A, current=B`, and the first turn fails as in step 3.

Rolling the thread back past the turn on A should clear it, because `thread_rollback` re-runs rollout reconstruction. I haven't verified this.

### What is the expected behavior?

Switching to a working model should let the thread continue. If compaction on the previous model fails with a non-retryable error, Codex should compact with the newly selected model. This should work for every provider and for both the local and remote compaction paths. At minimum, the thread should not stay pinned to a model the provider rejects.

### Additional information

Possible fixes, any of which would avoid the permanent failure:

- Apply the current-model retry from `should_retry_with_current_model` to all providers, and to the local `run_inline_auto_compact_task` path.
- When previous-model compaction fails with a permanent error (401, 403, 404, or model not supported), stop retrying it on later turns: replace or clear `previous_turn_settings`.
- Record a turn's model as previous only after a sampling request on it succeeds, so one rejected turn doesn't set the trap.

Related:
- #48949: the same missing fallback on Amazon Bedrock, where it shows up as a hang instead.
- #54226 and #54030: ChatGPT-auth threads stuck after the previous model was retired.

labels.name: app

items.body:
### App version

Older Windows Codex desktop installation; exact build was not captured. Reported October 15, 2026. The old model menu did not offer GPT-6.1 Sol. An affected user identified the outdated installation while finding the current Microsoft Store app/update. The original installation/update channel has not been independently verified.

### Subscription and platform

ChatGPT Plus; the desktop app itself displayed Plus. Windows; exact OS build not captured. Personal account identifiers are intentionally omitted.

### Problem

This report concerns update discovery and actionable error messages, related to the model rejection reported in #54234.

The affected user reports being unable to use any model available in the older Windows app for nearly two weeks, without seeing an update reminder or an obvious update option. They checked their email and found no update notification.

A screenshot reviewed on October 15 showed a basic prompt, the selected model “5.5 Medium,” a Plus badge, and this error:

> The 'gpt-5.5' model is not supported when using Codex with a ChatGPT account.

The message did not explain that an app update or model migration might be required, and did not provide an update link. Troubleshooting consequently focused on subscription/account mismatch, sign-in, and model switching, despite Plus being recognized. The old client did not expose the recommended replacement GPT-6.1 Sol.

### Observed workflow

These are user-reported observations, not an independent reproduction on a captured old build:

1. Open an existing older Windows Codex installation with a ChatGPT Plus account.
2. Select an available model and submit a basic prompt.
3. Receive the unsupported-model error. The user reports failures across all models offered by that installation.
4. Look for an update reminder or recovery guidance; none was visible to the user.
5. Discover the current Windows Store update separately and identify that the previous client lacked newer model choices.

### Expected behavior

- Detect when an installed client/model catalog is too old to offer supported models and show a prominent update notice with the correct Windows update route.
- Distinguish retired models and outdated clients from subscription/account entitlement errors.
- Identify a supported replacement and explain whether a client update is required.
- Provide advance notice when a compatibility change can leave an older client unusable. Please consider email or opted-in phone/push notifications alongside an in-app notice.
- Preserve projects and conversations through the supported update path.

### Context and diagnostic limits

Official documentation states GPT-5.5 retired from Codex with ChatGPT sign-in on October 14, 2026, with GPT-6.1 Sol recommended for Plus when available: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/models

That explains the pictured GPT-5.5 rejection but does not, by itself, explain the reported nearly two-week history or every other model failure. Please investigate client update/catalog behavior rather than treating retirement as a confirmed explanation for the whole incident.

The affected user attributes the issue to an outdated app with no update reminder. There is no verified finding that access to a particular distribution channel was deliberately revoked. Exact old/new versions, updater logs, and successful post-update inference were not captured.

Submitted with the affected user's explicit permission. No name, email, account ID, session ID, screenshot, local paths, or chat history is included.

items.title: Treat explicit connections to the verified default daemon as local
items.body:
Treat explicit connections to the verified default daemon as local

## Why

Explicitly selecting the default daemon socket previously classified the TUI connection as remote, changing how local configuration and thread parameters were handled. A socket at that path may also be an SSH forward, so the path alone cannot establish that the daemon is local.

## What changed

- Verify the default daemon endpoint before classifying an explicit connection as local. On Unix, check the expected symlink target and the private socket directory's ownership and permissions, then connect to the protected endpoint directly.
- Preserve local workspace behavior and local thread parameters for verified attachments while keeping directly bound Unix sockets classified as remote.
- Report a missing explicitly requested socket, disable embedded fallback for explicit attachments, and restrict daemon auto-start to implicit connections.

## Testing

Extend tests to cover explicit and implicit local target selection, verified socket resolution, and rejection of a directly bound socket as a local daemon endpoint.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1007.71326 (build 20398), read from the installed app bundle's Info.plist. I did not inspect the About dialog.

### What subscription do you have?

Unknown (current subscription not verified).

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm

### What issue are you seeing?

In one Codex App chat, the assistant treated Daybreak as if it required a separate model name. With GPT-6 Sol shown in the model picker, it said the absence of a distinct Daybreak model identifier meant it could not accept the task as a Daybreak review. After the user explained that Daybreak is a toggle, the assistant first treated that statement as proof of the effective mode, then reversed again and said the mode was unverified. Those contradictory answers interrupted the requested read-only review.

The model picker screenshot later showed the Daybreak switch on alongside GPT-6 Sol. Because that screenshot was captured after the earlier answers, it does not prove the effective Daybreak state of those earlier requests. This report is about the assistant's incorrect inference from the model label and inconsistent explanation. I have no evidence that request routing or Daybreak safeguards failed. No native error message appeared. Observed in one chat; not reproduced from a clean chat.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Open a Codex App task with a Daybreak-approved account.
2. In the Advanced model picker, select GPT-6 Sol and turn on the Daybreak switch before sending a request.
3. Ask the assistant to act as a Daybreak read-only reviewer and to identify only the model and mode it can actually observe.
4. In the affected chat, the assistant inferred from the lack of a separate Daybreak model identifier that it could not proceed as a Daybreak reviewer.
5. Tell the assistant that Daybreak is a toggle, not a separate model. In the affected chat, its explanation changed twice rather than consistently distinguishing the visible switch from independently verified request state.

This sequence describes one observed conversation, not a confirmed deterministic reproduction. No code is required.

Session ID: Not included in this public report; can be provided privately if needed.
Token limit usage: Not available.
Context window usage: Not available.

### What is the expected behavior?

The assistant should recognize that Daybreak is an independent request toggle and that GPT-6 Sol can be selected while Daybreak is on. It should not infer that Daybreak is off, unavailable, or invalid solely because the model label does not contain "Daybreak." If effective request-level Daybreak state is not exposed to the assistant, it should state that limit consistently and distinguish the user's visible UI setting from backend verification.

### Additional information

OpenAI's Daybreak overview says the Codex App uses a toggle in the Advanced model picker for a request and lists GPT-6 Sol as a supported mainline model: https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001258-openai-daybreak-trusted-access-for-cyber-overview

Related but distinct: #46605 reports missing Daybreak state for delegated reviewers. This report concerns the primary chat assistant's interpretation of the model picker and its inconsistent claims. The screenshot is omitted because it contains unrelated private conversation. No logs, account identifiers, repository names, or private task details are included.

items.body:
Skip SQLite page reclamation on Linux NFS mounts

## Why

SQLite page reclamation on NFS creates I/O load and contention.

## What changed

Detect whether `sqlite_home` is on NFS on Linux and skip reclamation before opening a maintenance connection. Cache successful filesystem probes across `SqliteConfig` clones while allowing failed probes to retry.

## Testing

Add tests for shared probe caching and recovery after a missing directory is created. Update reclamation coverage to expect no reclaimed pages or file shrinkage on NFS.

items.title: [macOS 26.1007.71326] 8.74 GiB main/renderer state plus agent-launched MLX transcription exhaust swap and reset WindowServer

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: model-behavior
labels.description: Issues related to behaviors exhibited by the model

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Codex Desktop `26.1007.71326` (build `20398`), bundled Codex `0.162.0-alpha.17.2`, Codex Framework `155.0.8059.40`.

### What subscription do you have?

Paid ChatGPT subscription; exact tier omitted from this public report.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 26.4.1 (25E253), Apple silicon Mac16,1, 16 GiB unified memory.

### What issue are you seeing?

A second system-wide memory incident occurred on October 16. Unlike my earlier #44996, this time a macOS watchdog stackshot preserved per-process memory at the time of failure. **The dominant Codex allocations were the desktop main process and renderer, not MCP helpers. A separate Python ML workload launched by Codex added another 5 GiB immediately before swap exhaustion. WindowServer then timed out and the desktop session was rebuilt, interrupting other applications.**

This report distinguishes three issues that need different investigation: large retained desktop state, the agent's resource-unaware choice of workload, and the OS-wide failure after swap could no longer grow. I am not claiming that all three have one implementation-level cause.

#### 1. Captured process footprints

The system stackshot covers `2026-10-16 04:50:23.588–04:50:29.491 +0800` (`2026-10-15 20:50:23.588–20:50:29.491 UTC`). Its `Footprint` fields report:

- ChatGPT/Codex desktop main process: **3270.41 MiB** (3.19 GiB), suspended.
- Largest, frontmost Codex renderer: **4551.54 MiB** (4.45 GiB).
- All 11 Codex renderers: **5679.47 MiB** (5.55 GiB).
- Main process plus all renderers: **8949.88 MiB** (8.74 GiB).
- Main bundled Codex app-server: **406.56 MiB**.
- 26 processes identified as Node/Node REPL with executable paths inside the installed ChatGPT bundle: **754.01 MiB** combined.
- All 47 processes with executable paths inside that bundle: **10876.86 MiB** (10.62 GiB) combined.
- Separate Python 3.12 inference process: **5094.32 MiB** (4.97 GiB).
- WindowServer itself: **1376.72 MiB**.

These are sums of Apple's per-process footprint fields, not an RSS snapshot or a claim that every summed byte is unique physical RAM. The Python value is separate from the 10.62 GiB bundle-path total. Process attribution is based on executable paths, not just display names.

The main process had been alive for 118274 seconds (32.85 hours). The large renderer had been alive for 118265 seconds. No current-incident renderer minidump/heap snapshot survived; the available stackshot shows the renderer repeatedly entering kernel/APFS/page-fault-related paths, while the main process had already been suspended by memory management. That establishes severe memory pressure, not the identity of a retaining JS object.

#### 2. The 5 GiB Python process was launched by the subtitle task

The task was to download a video and create reviewed bilingual subtitles using the existing YouTube automatic captions. Codex additionally chose to run local MLX Whisper over the entire audio as a cross-check.

The session transcript records this launch at `04:44:43.614 +0800`:

```text
work/asr-venv/bin/python work/check_audio.py > work/audio-check.log 2>&1
```

The original script at that point—not its later revised contents—called:

```python
mlx_whisper.transcribe(
    str(audio),
    path_or_hf_repo='mlx-community/whisper-large-v3-turbo',
    language='en',
    word_timestamps=True,
    verbose=False,
    initial_prompt='<interview context>',
)
```

Audio duration was 2374.381 seconds (39m34s); the original compressed audio was about 35 MiB. This was one full-audio inference worker, not an 80-process concurrency storm.

Attribution is supported by independent evidence:

- The stackshot identifies Python PID 68414, footprint 5094.32 MiB, with age 341 seconds. That places its start around `04:44:42.6`, within about a second of the recorded tool launch. The age field is rounded.
- System unified logs show PID 68414 contacting `cfprefsd` at `04:44:43.832` and `trustd` at `04:44:46.424`.
- The Python executable UUID in the stackshot is `4C4C449F-5555-3144-A18E-6A1A7C588299`; `dwarfdump --uuid` on that task's virtualenv interpreter resolves to the identical UUID. The virtualenv points to the uv-managed Python 3.12 executable.
- The recorded tool result returned shell session 35607 for this command. Later polling after the desktop session reset reported `Unknown process id 35607`.

This is a high-confidence correlation; the stackshot does not preserve the complete original PPID/argv chain, so I am not representing the UUID alone as unique to one task.

The package source explains why this was not a 35 MiB workload: `ModelHolder` keeps the model resident; the downloaded weights are about 1.5 GiB; the audio loader decodes the complete source, then computes the whole log-Mel spectrogram before windowed inference. A 16 kHz float32 waveform for the full source is about 145 MiB, and STFT/features/decoder intermediates add allocations. `word_timestamps=True` invokes another forward pass with cross-attention, stacking/normalizing alignment weights and converting them to NumPy for filtering/alignment. Those paths explain the allocation categories, but the available evidence cannot assign each part of the observed 5094.32 MiB to a particular tensor or allocator cache, or prove an MLX leak.

The model download took 2m34s according to the preserved tool output, so recognition started approximately `04:47:18`. Eleven seconds later, the kernel reported failure to create swap. The task polled transcription progress and model-download size but did not measure its own RSS, system memory pressure, or available disk space. It chose full-file large-model inference even though captions already existed and the immediate purpose was verification of names/phrases.

After the incident, the task changed its script at `04:53:33` to 300-second chunks, `word_timestamps=False`, and checkpoints. The new run completed at about `04:56`. That is a successful functional fallback, not a measured before/after memory benchmark. It must not be confused with what ran during the crash.

#### 3. Main/renderer retention and event fan-out

Seven retained desktop main-log segments cover this application lifetime from October 14 to the freeze. A bounded offline scan found:

- **9840 distinct completed reasoning item IDs, delivered 19989 times** across renderer views. 9003 items appeared twice, 573 three times, 264 once.
- **9593 deliveries** explicitly carried `rendererWindowVisible=false`. The latest recorded visibility state for ten non-primary webcontents was hidden; eleven renderer processes were present in the stackshot. Hidden does not establish that a window was closed or its renderer orphaned.
- **6156 `ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications` errors**, first at October 14 `11:59:29.162Z`, last at October 15 `20:47:00.201Z`—before the local model began inference. These are a UI-path symptom, not proof of memory retention by ResizeObserver itself.
- **3206 failed `durable` host reconnection attempts** during the same lifetime. The final retry at `04:47:24` again failed before WebSocket establishment. Request counters near the end showed no pending client/internal requests; the retry count alone therefore does not establish a pending-request memory leak.
- **400 distinct thread/server startup pairs across 92 thread IDs** over the lifetime. These are historical startup records, not 400 simultaneously live processes.
- **16 successful `inactive_thread_unsubscribed` events**. Cleanup does run in some cases; this is not evidence that every unsubscribe or archive leaks.
- Only **185 `thread/turns/list`** and **385 `thread/items/list`** responses over the retained lifetime. This does not show the rapid post-crash history-refetch storm described in #34890.

Two long-lived tasks streaming around the incident had pre-incident rollout sizes of 287045934 and 168225124 bytes. The first included about 210.57 MB of persisted compaction records; the second included about 62.22 MB of tool-output records and a single 8.51 MB tool-output record. The new subtitle task had only about 2.69 MB of persisted history before the freeze.

These file sizes are context, **not proof that the entire JSONL/compaction corpus was loaded into the live UI**. They do show why task-count limits do not bound the size of individual retained conversations and why the newly started subtitle task alone is unlikely to explain the desktop UI footprint.

#### 4. Read-only inspection of the shipped desktop code

I inspected the installed `app.asar` by reading individual archive members without changing the application:

- `.vite/build/src-DCNiwad_.js` contains the conversation-manager/inactivity logic. The inactivity constants are `Zb=108e5` (3 hours) and `$b=10` retained inactive owner conversations. `getInactiveOwnerConversationIdsToUnsubscribe` excludes active views, owned stream followers, and conversations for which `shouldKeepConversationLoaded` is true.
- `shouldKeepConversationLoaded` protects active/in-progress runtimes and pending interaction items. `releaseInactivePassiveConversation` also skips conversations with a stream role, active view, pending requests, or keep-loaded status.
- A successful unsubscribe clears turn data only under additional eligibility conditions. Full `conversationCacheEvictor` removal is called by archive/delete/discard paths. The inspected inactivity policy is based on age/count/state, not a byte budget.
- The same manager/history code is present in `webview/assets/app-shared-8340f229c2b3.js`. It processes `item/completed` and updates the conversation's turn/item state; live logs independently confirm delivery to multiple renderer views, including hidden ones.
- The IPC `sendBroadcast` path serializes the message using `JSON.stringify` and obtains its byte length before rejecting frames over 268435456 bytes. This is the same allocation-risk ordering reported in #52631, but **there are zero oversized-broadcast warnings in this incident's retained logs**. I cannot claim that path caused the observed main-process allocation.

The supported interpretation is retained/replicated large conversation state plus long-lived windows as a likely contributing path. **There is no surviving heap profile or retained-object graph proving what exact objects account for 3.19 GiB main-process and 4.45 GiB primary-renderer memory.** A heap/native allocation capture from an instrumented build is needed to close that gap. Claiming an exact object-level root cause from the stackshot would overstate the evidence.

#### 5. Kernel-confirmed failure timeline

All times below are October 16, UTC+08:00:

```text
04:44:43.614  Agent launches full-audio MLX Whisper worker.
~04:47:18     Model download finishes; full-audio recognition begins.
04:47:28.325  Last retained desktop main-log line.
04:47:29.562  kernel: low swap: failed to create swapfile
04:47:30.246  kernel: memorystatus: suspending ChatGPT [41084] due to swap exhaustion
04:47:35.288  kernel: suspending WeChat due to swap exhaustion
04:47:40.311  kernel: suspending MailMaster due to swap exhaustion
04:47:45.388  kernel: suspending Google Chrome due to swap exhaustion
04:47:50.388  kernel: suspending D-Chat due to swap exhaustion
...          More unrelated apps are suspended; compressor-space-shortage repeats.
04:50:23.588  System stackshot begins.
04:50:46.902  watchdogd saves WindowServer userspace_watchdog_timeout report.
~04:51       New loginwindow/desktop session and application processes start.
```

The watchdog report says WindowServer's main work processor had not checked in for 40 seconds. This was a desktop-session reset, not a full reboot: kernel boot time remained October 13. During diagnosis after the session reset, the data volume reported 99% used and about 8.2 GiB available. That is a material environmental contributor to swap-growth failure; its exact free-space value before the incident was not captured, so I am not claiming disk fullness alone caused it.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

No deliberate replay to system failure was attempted.

Observed workflow:

1. Keep the macOS desktop app running for about 33 hours while working in several long-lived, tool-heavy local conversations and secondary windows.
2. Continue three visible user tasks; other views remain hidden. The desktop continues to deliver completed-item events to multiple views.
3. Ask for reviewed bilingual subtitles using an available YouTube caption track.
4. Codex additionally installs MLX Whisper and launches full-file `whisper-large-v3-turbo` inference with word timestamps on a 39-minute source without measuring current machine headroom.
5. With large pre-existing desktop state and limited free disk, model loading/recognition is followed by swapfile creation failure, mass application suspension, and a WindowServer watchdog timeout.

### What is the expected behavior?

- Main-process and renderer memory should remain bounded during long-running, multi-window work, including active large conversations and replicated/follower state.
- Desktop reclamation should account for retained bytes, not only inactive-task count and age. Hidden/follower views should not unnecessarily retain full histories or redundant state.
- An agent should choose a resource-appropriate verification method: use the existing captions and targeted ambiguous excerpts rather than unconditionally running a large model over the entire source. Local ML workload selection should account for current memory and disk pressure.
- Please provide a supported way to capture main/renderer heap and native-memory attribution before the next failure, and investigate which state/IPC allocation path retains the observed memory.

### Additional information

Related issues reviewed:

- #44996 is my earlier macOS swap-exhaustion incident. This new report has a different dominant memory breakdown and a separately identified agent-launched ML workload. It should not be treated as proof that archive cleanup failed.
- #34890 covers multi-task renderer memory, fan-out and crash/reload behavior; this incident has a system stackshot but no renderer minidump/refetch storm.
- #52631 has confirmed main-process V8 heap OOM and oversized IPC payload warnings. This incident has large main-process footprint but no matching warning or confirmed V8 OOM trap.
- #53277 covers a Windows renderer memory spike and denied hydration; there are no matching denied-hydration errors here.
- #37653 covers agent-generated MLX workload concurrency failures. Here one full-file worker was sufficient to add about 5 GiB; the trigger was not broken parallel-job counting.

Public evidence is sanitized. Raw stackshots/logs/session files contain other applications, prompts, proprietary project material, local paths and authentication-related metadata and are not uploaded. The preserved watchdog report is the `2026-10-16-045046` WindowServer `userspace_watchdog_timeout.spin` report. Targeted sanitized excerpts or an instrumented capture can be supplied if maintainers identify the fields needed.

items.title: Managed daemon needs an atomic idle-only relaunch that never force-kills admitted work

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
A local operator cannot safely implement an idle-only relaunch by checking `thread/loaded/list` plus every `thread/read` and then running `codex app-server daemon bootstrap`.

Source at `rust-v0.162.1`:

1. `app-server-daemon/src/lib.rs::bootstrap_locked` holds the lifecycle operation lock, stops the updater and calls `stop_with_grace` on the daemon.
2. `backend/pid.rs::stop_with_grace` sends SIGTERM and escalates to SIGKILL when the grace period expires. A second forceable shutdown signal can also force the server's drain.
3. `app-server/src/turn_admission.rs` protects turn admission with its own lock. The daemon lifecycle lock does not stop a connected client from starting work between an operator's idle inventory and shutdown.

A detached worker can remain active after its terminal has disappeared. Connected client counts do not prove idleness. Increasing a grace timeout does not make an idle snapshot atomic and still permits forced interruption.

Requested behavior: a native conditional lifecycle operation that verifies the expected daemon identity and zero active/unknown work while atomically closing new thread/turn admission, then replaces daemon and updater with the requested minimum inherited soft limit. A racing admission must either be rejected before it starts, or make the relaunch refuse. No timeout, retry, or already-draining condition may turn this into a forced kill. Preserve remote-control and update settings.

Regression cases should include: active detached thread; incomplete/unknown inventory; a turn racing the idle check; stale/replaced PID; an already-draining daemon; and preservation of higher limits and existing remote/update settings. This request is based on the source race and an observed operational interruption; no new live restart was performed to reproduce it.

items.title: Allow root turn suspension with live descendants
items.body:
Allow root turn suspension with live descendants

## Why

Live descendants previously blocked suspension of an unfinished root turn, requiring callers to stop and unload them before recovering the root elsewhere.

## What changed

Allow `suspend_turn_and_shutdown` to suspend the root and initiate shutdown of all sessions sharing its local agent runtime, fencing new starts. Remove `SuspendTurnOutcome::HasLiveDescendants`.

Success confirms that the root has stopped and its history writer is flushed and closed; descendant cleanup completes separately. Callers must finish tree shutdown or fence and terminate the tree's persistence writers before transferring ownership. Interrupted descendants are not automatically recovered.

## Testing

Extend integration coverage to verify child shutdown, recovery under the original root turn ID without restarting children, and separate reporting of child writer failures.

### Component
ChatGPT/Codex desktop app on macOS, using the official ChatGPT Sites publishing workflow. App version not collected.

### Problem
The permissions control in the affected chat visibly shows **Ask for approval** selected (confirmed by a user-provided screenshot). However, submitting the required input to the official Sites source workflow via `write_stdin` fails without presenting a manual approval prompt:

```text
write_stdin rejected: approval required by policy, but AskForApproval::Granular.sandbox_approval is false
```

### Reproduction steps observed
1. Build and locally test a private Sites application.
2. Grant requested network access and source-repository filesystem access through `request_permissions`.
3. Start the official `site-workflow.mjs --project-id <existing-project-id>` helper using `exec_command` with `tty: true`.
4. Wait for `Ready for Site workflow JSON on stdin (input is hidden).`
5. Submit the required credential/configuration JSON via `write_stdin` (credentials omitted here).
6. Observe the error above. No manual approval prompt appears.

Repeated attempts, including a fresh helper process after granting permissions, produced the same rejection. A retry after the user was advised to restart also failed; actual restart completion was not independently verified.

### Expected behavior
The selected approval mode and effective execution policy should agree, or the desktop app should clearly identify an overriding restriction and provide an actionable supported resolution. The official publishing helper should either operate within granted permissions or expose the required approval prompt.

### Additional observations
- Permission grants succeeded; a grant response included `strict_auto_review: true`.
- The effective session instructions reported granular `sandbox_approval`, `rules`, and `skill_approval` categories disabled, while `request_permissions` and `mcp_elicitations` could prompt.
- Local application builds and tests passed. Publication was blocked before source synchronization.
- It is not established whether this reflects managed-policy precedence, a UI/session state mismatch, or interactive-input permission handling.

### Impact
Unable to complete private Sites publication despite an apparently selected interactive approval mode and explicit network/filesystem permission grants.

This report intentionally omits account emails, application/customer details, project identifiers, credentials, source code, raw logs, and conversation transcripts. The user authorized this sanitized public report.
